{{Short description|Semantic interpretations of language}}
In [[linguistics]], '''exhaustivity''' is the phenomenon where a [[proposition]] can be strengthened with the [[logical negation|negation]] of certain alternatives. For example, in response to the question "Which students got an A?", the utterance "Ava got an A" has an '''exhaustive interpretation''' when it conveys that no other students got an A. It has a '''non-exhaustive interpretation''' when it merely conveys that Ava was among the students who got an A.

Exhaustivity is a major topic in the linguistic subfields of [[semantics_(linguistics)|semantics]] and [[pragmatics]]. Research on the topic aims to explain when and why expressions receive exhaustive interpretations. Particular factors include [[focus_(linguistics)|focus]],{{sfnm|1a1=Rooth|1y=1992|2a1=Rooth|2y=2016}} [[disjunction]],{{sfnm|1a1=Chierchia|1a2=Fox|1a3=Spector|1y=2012|2a1=Chierchia|2y=2004|3a1=Fox|3y=2007}} [[questions]],{{sfn|Karttunen|Peters|1979}} and [[polarity items]].{{sfnm|1a1=Krifka|1y=1995|2a1=Chierchia|2y=2013}} A major theoretical issue is whether exhaustivity is a semantic [[entailment]] encoded in the [[grammar]], a pragmatic [[implicature]] arising from [[Gricean]] [[social cognition]], or some combination of the two.{{sfn|Grice|1975}}{{sfnm|1a1=Chierchia|1a2=Fox|1a3=Spector|1y=2012|2a1=Chierchia|2y=2013|2pp=100-33}}
